background.definition: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) is a life-threatening endocrine emergency manifested by marked elevation of blood glucose, hyperosmolarity, and little or no ketosis. It is one end of the continuum of hyperglycemic crisis (with diabetic ketoacidosis at the other end) with about one third of the patients manifesting characteristics of both.

list.listitem: In the United States, around 1% of hospitalizations for patients with diabetes are due to hyperglycemic crisis, with HHS accounting for 35% of cases, DKA 38%, and mixed DKA/HHS 27%. HHS mortality is 5- to 10-fold higher compared to DKA despite improvements in treatment of the two conditions.
Increasing prevalence in children, especially with obesity and a family history of type 2 DM.

The most common precipitating cause is underlying infection, especially pneumonia and urinary tract infections. Noncompliance, lack of access to medical care, or inadequate monitoring of blood sugar are also important contributing factors. See for other causes of HHS.
In a series of 119 Chinese patients with HHS, the precipitating cause was infection in 57%, poor compliance with medication in 21%, and undiagnosed diabetes in 11%.
Initial relative insulin deficiency.
Glucosuric diuresis, which impairs concentrating capacity of the kidney, which leads to further water loss .

Increase in insulin counter regulatory hormones (cortisol, catecholamines, glucagon, and growth hormone) causes increased hepatic and renal glucose production and impaired glucose utilization in the peripheral tissues.
Continued water loss, which is greater than sodium loss, which leads to the hyperosmolarity.
There is enough circulating insulin present to prevent lipolysis (release of free fatty acids from adipose tissue) and unrestrained hepatic fatty acid oxidation to ketone bodies.
Diagnosis is made with a combination of marked elevation of blood glucose (greater than 600 mg/dL) and elevation in serum osmolarity (greater than 320 mOsm/L) with little or no ketosis. C
Patients may complain of weakness, visual disturbance, leg cramps, nausea, vomiting, confusion, lethargy with physical findings of profound dehydration. C
Carefully evaluate for precipitating factors, especially infection, noncompliance with medications and coexisting diseases. C
HHS usually evolves over days to weeks.

Symptoms of hyperglycemia preceding the hyperosmolar state include polydipsia, polyuria, polyphagia, weight loss, abdominal pain, and vomiting. With increasing dehydration patients develop weakness, changes in mental status, and coma. The presence of stupor or coma in the absence of definitive evidence of a hyperosmolar state (serum osmolality >320 mEq/L) should prompt a search for alternative causes.

Physical findings may include signs of dehydration (poor skin turgor, dry mucous membranes, orthostatic findings). Temperature is commonly normal or hypothermic, even in the face of infection, because of peripheral vasodilatation.
A diagnostic evaluation for HHS should be undertaken when a patient presents with altered mental status, with or without the previous diagnosis of type 2 diabetes.

The initial evaluation which aids in diagnosing HHS and differentiating it from diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) should include the blood glucose level, calculated serum osmolarity, serum electrolytes, arterial blood gas (ABG) (to assess arterial pH), serum bicarbonate, serum ketones, calculated anion gap, CBC including differential, and ECG (see and ).

The blood glucose and serum osmolarity are essential in making the diagnosis, with the blood glucose usually above 600 mg/dL and the effective serum osmolarity greater than 320 mOsm/kg (Calculation: 2(measured Na(mEq/L))+glucose(mg/dL)/18).
Serum electrolytes are essential in the management. Low or normal serum potassium on admission suggests total body potassium deficiency and require close cardiac monitoring and potassium replacement.
ABGs, serum bicarbonate, serum ketones, urine ketones by dipstick, and calculated anion gap are essential in differentiating HHS from DKA ().
CBC important for consideration of underlying causes, eg, sepsis, but note that leukocytosis does increase directly with the degree of ketosis.
EKG/ monitoring important for diagnosis of rhythm disturbance secondary to hypokalemia or diagnosis of underlying ischemic event.
Urinalysis necessary to look for underlying urinary tract infection.
Additional tests may include CXR, bacterial cultures of urine, blood, throat, sputum, etc, as clinically indicated.
HgbA1C may be useful in determining the evolution of the problem, eg, newly diagnosed versus acute exacerbation of previously well controlled DM.
Consider HHS and check the blood glucose when patients present with neurologic symptoms, even with no history of diabetes.

The initial evaluation should include the blood glucose level, calculated serum osmolarity, serum electrolytes, ABG, serum bicarbonate, serum ketones, calculated anion gap, CBC including differential, and ECG.
See for guidelines regarding distinguishing HHS from diabetic ketoacidosis, and for a suggested approach to management.

Dehydration is profound (average 9 L in adults) and the volume should be replaced in the ICU within 24 hours in adults, 48 hours in children with frequent monitoring of blood glucose and electrolytes. B
Begin with 0.9% normal saline and add potassium and adjust fluids based upon clinical and laboratory response. B
After fluids have begun, add initial insulin bolus followed by continuous IV insulin drip. B

There is a five-pronged approach to successful treatment: vigorous IV replacement, electrolyte replacement, IV insulin, diagnosis and management of preexisting and coexisting causes, and prevention (see ). The average fluid deficit is 9 L (100-200 mL/kg).

Calculate the corrected serum sodium as the elevated glucose falsely lowers the measured sodium. Calculation: corrected serum sodium = measured serum sodium + 1.65 x ((glucose in mg/dL − 100)/100). During the first hour, give 0.9% saline at a rate of 15-20 mL/kg (approximately 1-1.5 L) in adults. The choice of the following fluids depends on the corrected serum sodium, if low continue the 0.9% saline but if normal or elevated change to 0.45% saline at a rate of 4-14 mL/kg/h. Replace the calculated fluid deficit in 24 hours.

If serum potassium is <3.3 mEq/L and renal function is established, hold insulin and give 20-40 mEq/L potassium, given 2/3 as KCl and 1/3 KPO4 until potassium ≥3.3 mEq/L. If serum potassium is >5.0 mEq/L, do not add potassium but check serum potassium every 2 hours. Once renal function is assured, and the potassium is <5 and ≥3.3, the infusion should contain 20-40 mEq/L potassium, given 2/3 as KCl and 1/3 KPO4. Maintain serum potassium between 4 and 5 mEq/L.

Careful monitoring of the blood glucose, hemodynamic state, cardiac, renal, mental status, and electrolytes must be performed, especially in those with underlying renal or cardiac compromise. Induced change in osmolarity should not exceed 3 mOsm/kg H2O/h.
Once the serum glucose reaches 300 mg/dL, change the fluid to D5 in 0.45% NS to maintain glucose between 250 and 300 mg/dL, until the serum osmolality is <315 mOsm/kg and the patient is alert.

Insulin therapy should begin after fluids have begun, water follows glucose intracellularly leading to a potential for worsened hypotension. Insulin should be withheld until the potassium is greater than 3.3 mEq/L. An initial bolus of insulin of 0.15 units/kg body wt followed by a continuous infusion of regular insulin at 0.1 unit/kg/h.
If an inadequate response (less than 50-75 mg/h) is not achieved, the continuous dose of IV insulin may be doubled.

Once the blood glucose level is less than 300 mg/dL, the fluids may be changed to D5 half normal saline (as above) and the continuous dose of insulin may be decreased to 0.05 units/h until mental changes have cleared and hyperosmolarity has resolved. Institution of sliding scale insulin and conversion to home regimens may then occur.
Bicarbonate should not be utilized in the treatment of HHS.
Identify and treat the causative factors precipitating the event.
Prevention of future events is extremely important.
After discharge, frequent home glucose monitoring occurs, utilizing family members, caregivers, and others for frequent observations regarding fluid intake and mental status changes.
Complications from undertreatment include vascular occlusions, eg, mesenteric thrombosis, myocardial infarction, low flow syndrome, and disseminated intravascular coagulopathy.

Complications from overtreatment include adult respiratory distress syndrome and hypoglycemia. Cerebral edema (suggested by a headache and a sudden decrease in level of consciousness) is treated with IV mannitol (1-2 g/kg over 30 minutes) and IV dexamethasone. Slowing the rate of correction of hyperosmolarity may prevent cerebral edema.
Mortality rate in HHS ranges form 10% to 25% in various series. B
Predictors of a fatal outcome include extremes of age, degree of dehydration, hemodynamic instability, underlying precipitating causes, and degree of consciousness. B
Careful outpatient follow-up is important to ensure compliance with medication, appropriate blood sugar monitoring, adequate hydration, and early treatment of acute infections. C

Increased rates of childhood obesity are linked to an increased prevalence of type 2 diabetes in children and adolescents with nearly 4% of newly diagnosed pediatric type 2 DM patients presenting with HHS.
While onset of HHS in adults is gradual (averaging 12 days), the onset in children is usually less than 1 week.
Evidence-based guidelines for pediatric HHS do not exist.

Consider HHS and order a blood glucose in children who have vague symptoms of headache, abdominal pain, weakness, nausea/vomiting, who are obese, and have a family history of type 2 DM especially if signs of insulin resistance (acanthosis nigricans).

There is an increased incidence of cerebral edema, which may be fatal in children. The etiology is unclear, probably ischemic. Intensive care admission is recommended with hourly monitoring of glucose and electrolytes avoiding overly rapid correction to help avoid cerebral edema.
Case reports of a malignant hyperthermia-like syndrome have been reported in children with HHS treated with dantrolene.
